title: Resume batches and recover interrupted items
description: A batch can be interrupted by a crash, a closed terminal or a signal. Restarting must continue the queued work without repeating a review whose prompt may already have been delivered, and without silently discarding the uncertain item.
design:
batch resume BATCH_ID [--skip-run=RUN_ID] [--json]:

- Obtain the batch ownership lock and load the frozen queue. Never re-read the list file or current defaults as instructions for old items.
- Completed and failed items stay recorded and are not run again. Queued items keep their allocated IDs and setting records.
- An interrupted item is not an unstarted item. If spawn or send could have happened, stop with RECOVERY_REQUIRED and show the run, pass, pane, session, prompt hash and available cursors, so the human can inspect the pane or discuss the session.
- --skip-run=RUN_ID continues the queued items while leaving that interrupted item explicitly unresolved. Accept it only for the interrupted item blocking that batch. Preserve its record and live pane. Never claim the skipped item succeeded or did no work.
- If a prepared item has a durable checkpoint proving no spawn was attempted, it can return to queued. A spawning checkpoint is not that proof.
- Add no reset, force-complete or automatic pass-replay command. To repeat a failed review, create a new run with a new session and ID.
- SIGINT/SIGTERM during a batch follows the single-run interrupt rules and keeps the uncertain item.
acceptance_criteria:
- T314: interrupt a batch during a pass -> uncertain item retained; no replay.
- T315: resume with queued items -> finished and failed items unchanged.
- T316: skip the blocking interrupted item -> explicit skipped/unresolved result; queued items continue.
- Resume never re-reads the repository list.
- Resume of a batch with an uncertain spawning item and no --skip-run exits with RECOVERY_REQUIRED.

title: Open a saved session in a discussion pane
description: After a review the user wants to talk with the agent about the results, in the same Claude session that did the review, without replaying any pass and without ever falling back to a blank session that knows nothing about the review.
design:
sessions open RUN_ID [--json]:

- First check that the run is no longer owned by a worker. Refuse while the automated review is active.
- If the recorded pane is still live on the selected server, report its target. Do not start a second process for the same session. A pane that is working or awaiting approval is reported as such; never send into it.

Use the original repository cwd and the recorded vendor config root, the recorded agent settings and the added directories. Do not pass --session-id, --continue or --fork-session. Do not send a prompt, rerun a pass, rerun lint or remove scratch.

- If resume fails, keep the saved record and return SESSION_UNAVAILABLE. Never turn a resume failure into a new blank review session. If the config root or session is absent or unreadable, fail; never fall back to another account or a substitute session.

title: Author docs/DESIGN_PHILOSOPHY.md
description: The project's intent — why it was built, what it is really for, and the taste rules that constrain its evolution — is undocumented. The single most valuable outcome of a review (a conversational partner deeply primed on the target repo) is stated nowhere. Without a canonical statement of what the project is trying to be, future maintainers and agents proposing changes have no anchor and risk pulling the tool away from its human-facing purpose. This doc makes the philosophy first-class and load-bearing.
design:
Create `docs/DESIGN_PHILOSOPHY.md` (this is the step that creates the `docs/` folder). Human-facing prose in the project's voice — direct, opinionated, for a careful human reader (the register of the README and the prompt prose). Target ~1–2 pages. Six required sections, each carrying this load-bearing content (phrasing is the writer's to choose):

1. **Genesis — what it was first.** A short series of prompt files whose only job was to help its author understand *someone else's* codebase. The author understood every line of every prompt; comprehensibility was the point. Not a code review, not a security audit — each pass interrogates a different layer of how an author thinks.
2. **The payoff — a primed conversational partner (the biggest human value).** The most valuable outcome is not the written analysis but that, afterward, you are talking to an agent deeply primed on the repo. When the target has an interesting "smell" or "taste," these become genuinely productive, abstract, high-level conversations. The methodology exists to manufacture that partner; when the repo is "juicy," that is where the value lands.
3. **Optionality and low commitment.** After the first couple of analytical passes the user picks and chooses which (if any) later passes to run, and can put the whole review down if it isn't earning its keep. Early termination is a *feature*, not a failure — a pass that stops with a real finding beats one that fabricates output.
4. **Two faces — human and agentic.** The original tool was purely human-facing: canonical prose, read by a person, pick-and-choose. A later addition gave it an *agentic face* — machine-consumable structured output (the YAML appendix) so a review can be produced and consumed more autonomously by agents. The project now serves both readers with one discipline.
5. **The balance and the boundary rule (load-bearing).** Future improvements must not let the agentic face pull away from the human face. The rule: **the agentic face must speak the human face's idiom — prose, Markdown, or YAML. JSON is the boundary.** The structured appendix is YAML *not* JSON for exactly this reason. Route every "make it machine-consumable" proposal through one test: can it be expressed in an artifact a human would also read? 6. **Taste rules / design filters.** The short list every change is checked against: prose stays canonical / structure stays thin; no compliance bloat; the validators check *structure*, never analytical quality; no pass anticipates a later pass; improvements are accretive increments, not new product surfaces.
